stance_line: Wanting proof, but willing: ask for the plain thing first and see what comes back.
message:
Piotr here. I've got about three hundred markdown notes in one folder tree. I tidied them last month and now I can't tell which links still go anywhere. I want one small tool that tells me.

What I want first:

1. **Run it once, get a list.** I type `python3 linkcheck.py notes/` and it prints one line per dead link: the file, the line number, and the link as written. For example `Rings.md:14: [the family](Family.md)`. It exits non-zero if it found any and zero if it found none. It never writes to anything.

2. **Files, in whatever folder they've been moved to.** It follows ordinary markdown links like `[text](Shoes.md)`, `[text](../Prep/First Call.md)` and `[text](sub/Shoes.md)`. Paths are relative to the file the link is in. It also handles names with spaces, written as `First%20Call.md` or `<First Call.md>`. A link to a file that isn't there is dead. A link that lands on a folder is dead too. Web links (`http`, `https`) and `mailto:` are not checked and not counted.

3. **Headings.** I mark headings with `#` signs. `[text](Shoes.md#Laying out)` or `[text](#Laying-out)` is dead if that heading isn't in that file. Tell me in plain words how it matches a heading to the link text, for example case and spaces versus dashes. Keep it to one simple rule.

4. **A last line I can check against my own sense of things.** It prints how many files it read, how many links it checked, and how many were dead. If it read 0 files, it says so loudly and exits non-zero. A wrong folder name must not look like a clean bill of health.

5. **A test folder made on purpose, kept in the project.** It should hold a small set of notes with a known list of dead and good links, including some awkward good ones: a `../` link, a nested folder, a name with a space, a link to a heading, a link inside a code block, and a heading link on a note that has two headings the same. Put a plain list next to it saying which links are dead and why. I'll compare that list against what the tool prints. The tests should use that folder.

Limits:

- One file, `linkcheck.py`, plus its tests. I should be able to read all of it in one sitting.
- No options I have to learn. `--help` is fine, but the tool has to work with just the folder name.
- Nothing clever. No guessing what I meant, no "did you mean" suggestions, no fixing anything.
- If it isn't sure whether a link is good, say in the usage text how it decides. Don't hide it.
- My notes sometimes say "see Shoes" in the text. I don't know if that counts as a link for this tool. Tell me plainly which link forms it recognises and which it ignores, in the usage text. Don't quietly pick.
- It never changes my files.

New requirements, build them together:
- Running `python3 linkcheck.py <folder>` prints one line per broken internal link as `file:line: link-as-written`, exits non-zero if any are broken and zero if none, and writes nothing anywhere but stdout. (I will check: Run it on the test folder; compare the printed lines to the expected-broken list, and check the exit code is non-zero. Run it on a folder with no broken links and see exit 0.)
- File links are resolved relative to the file containing them, including ../ and nested folders and names with spaces (%20 or <...>); missing files and links landing on a folder are broken; http, https and mailto links are neither checked nor counted. (I will check: Test folder contains good and dead examples of each of these; the tool flags exactly the dead ones.)
- Heading links (file.md#Heading and #Heading) are broken if the target file has no matching # heading, using one simple matching rule that the usage text states in plain words. (I will check: Test folder has good and dead heading links, including a note with two identical headings; the output matches the expected list, and --help states the rule.)
- After the list, it prints a summary of files read, links checked and links broken; if it reads zero files it says so loudly and exits non-zero. (I will check: Run on the test folder and see counts I can sanity check; run on a nonexistent or empty folder and see a loud message plus non-zero exit.)
- A purpose-built test folder lives in the project with a plain-language list of which links are broken and why, and the unit tests use it, covering relative paths, nested directories, heading anchors, links to missing files, and a link inside a code block; usage text states which link forms are recognised and which ignored (including plain 'see Shoes' text). (I will check: I read the expected list beside the folder and can follow it; python3 -m unittest passes; --help names the recognised and ignored link forms.)
new: Running `python3 linkcheck.py <folder>` prints one line per broken internal link as `file:line: link-as-written`, exits non-zero if any are broken and zero if none, and writes nothing anywhere but stdout.

File links are resolved relative to the file containing them, including ../ and nested folders and names with spaces (%20 or <...>); missing files and links landing on a folder are broken; http, https and mailto links are neither checked nor counted.
Heading links (file.md#Heading and #Heading) are broken if the target file has no matching # heading, using one simple matching rule that the usage text states in plain words.
After the list, it prints a summary of files read, links checked and links broken; if it reads zero files it says so loudly and exits non-zero.

stance_line: Works on its own folder. I want to see it fail on a messy one before I believe it.
message:
Good. Seven dead, matches your list, tests pass. I read the output, it's plain.

Two of your assumptions I don't accept.

1. A link with a title, [t](Shoes.md "title"), showing dead. That's a working link reported as broken, the one thing I said I can't have. Treat the title as a title and check Shoes.md.
2. Any existing file counts as good, even outside my notes folder. A link that climbs out of the folder is not a link my printout on the bus will follow. Report it as broken.

I'm fine with the rest: images count, Notes-1 is dead, exit 2 for nothing read. Keep them in --help.

I'm adding these. Limits: still one file plus tests, stdlib only, and nothing written but stdout. Don't add options or flags. If you want to add a knob, tell me why first.

Also tell me plainly two things I couldn't see: did the test folder have a link inside a code fence, and what happens with shoes.md when the file is Shoes.md? I want the answer in --help, not in your reply.

New requirements, build them together:
- A link with a title, [t](Shoes.md "title") or with single quotes, is checked as Shoes.md and is not reported when Shoes.md exists. Same for a heading link with a title. (I will check: testnotes gets one good titled link and one titled link to a missing file; only the missing one appears in the output and testnotes_EXPECTED.txt is updated to match.)
- A link that resolves to a place outside the folder given on the command line is reported as broken, even if a file exists there. (I will check: testnotes gets a link like ../../linkcheck.py from a nested note; it appears in the list and in the expected file with the reason.)
- Each broken line ends with a short plain reason after the link: no such file, is a folder, no such heading, or outside the folder. (I will check: Running on testnotes, each of the broken lines shows one of those reasons, and the expected file's reasons agree with them.)
- Heading matching is stated in --help with an example that includes punctuation, and behaves as stated: a heading like '# Rings, and who signs?' is matched by the link #Rings, and who signs? and by the dash form, and matching is not affected by trailing spaces or Windows line endings. (I will check: testnotes has a note saved with Windows line endings and a punctuated heading, linked from two other notes; they are not reported. The --help paragraph shows the example.)
- A second folder, testnotes_messy, imitates a real tidy-up: about 25 short notes in nested folders, some renamed or moved so their links died, Polish letters in file names (e.g. Załoba.md), a 'see Shoes' plain-text mention, a link in a code fence, an http link, a link with %20, a duplicate heading, and one link to a note that does not exist yet (like Rings to Family). It has its own plain-language expected list and a test that compares the tool's output to it. (I will check: I run the tool on testnotes_messy and get exactly the lines in its expected file; the count of files and links in the summary matches a count written at the top of that file.)
